title: Text Cleaning, Duplicates, and Missing Data
summary: Clean text columns with the .str accessor, remove duplicate rows with drop_duplicates, and handle missing values with isna, dropna, and fillna.

steps.title: Cleaning a text column with the .str accessor
steps.lede: Mixed-case and padded city names cause mismatches. The .str accessor applies string methods across an entire column at once.

blocks.text: Suppose the `city` column in a SwiftDrop export has `"Lagos"`, `" lagos"`, and `"LAGOS "` scattered across different rows — the same city, written three inconsistent ways. Grouping or filtering by city will miss rows until the values are standardised.

A Series' `.str` accessor lets you call ordinary string-processing methods — matching the names of Python's built-in string methods such as `lower`, `strip`, and `replace` — on every element of the Series at once: `orders["city"].str.strip().str.lower()` removes stray whitespace and lowercases every city value in one chained call, turning all three variants into the same `"lagos"`.

annotations.text: .str.strip() removes leading/trailing spaces; .str.lower() lowercases every value
All three variants now collapse to the same lowercase form

blocks.change_summary: city column cleaned: stray whitespace stripped and all values lowercased in one chained .str call.

public.prompt: You have a `city` column with mixed case and stray spaces: `[' Lagos', 'ABUJA ', 'Kano']`. Which code cleans every value to lowercase with no leading or trailing spaces?

opt_a.message: Correct. The `.str` accessor applies string methods like `strip()` and `lower()` to every element of the Series at once.

opt_b.message: Not quite. `.strip()` and `.lower()` are string methods that work on a single string, not a Series. Use the `.str` accessor to apply them to every element: `orders['city'].str.strip().str.lower()`.

opt_c.message: A Series does not have `.lower()` or `.strip()` directly. Use the `.str` accessor: `orders['city'].str.strip().str.lower()`.

opt_d.message: There is no `.str.clean()` method. Use `.str.strip()` to remove whitespace and `.str.lower()` to convert to lowercase.

correct.message: Exactly. The `.str` accessor lets you chain string methods to clean every value in a column.

incorrect.message: Not quite. Review how the `.str` accessor applies string methods across a column.

steps.title: Removing duplicate rows with drop_duplicates
steps.lede: A repeated order_id means the same order was logged twice. drop_duplicates removes the extra row, keeping the occurrence you choose.

blocks.text: Suppose order `#1003` appears twice in the SwiftDrop orders DataFrame, logged the same way both times. Any count or aggregation will be inflated until the duplicate is removed.

`duplicated()` returns a boolean vector indicating which rows are duplicates, and `drop_duplicates()` removes them; both accept a `subset` argument naming the columns used to identify a duplicated row: `orders.drop_duplicates(subset=["order_id"])` removes rows that repeat the same `order_id`.

By default, `drop_duplicates()` keeps the first occurrence of each duplicate set and drops the rest. Passing `keep='last'` keeps the last occurrence instead; `keep=False` drops every row that is part of a duplicate set: `orders.drop_duplicates(subset=["order_id"], keep="last")` would keep order `#1003`'s second logged row instead of its first.

before.caption: orders before deduplication — order_id 1003 appears twice

after.code:
orders_clean = orders.drop_duplicates(subset=["order_id"])
print(len(orders_clean))  # one row per order_id

annotations.text: subset=["order_id"] means two rows with the same order_id count as duplicates
Result has one row per unique order_id; first occurrence kept by default

blocks.change_summary: Duplicate order rows removed by drop_duplicates(subset=['order_id']); first occurrence kept.

opt_d.message: There is no `is_duplicate()` method. Use `duplicated(subset=['order_id'])` to identify duplicate rows.

correct.message: Exactly. The `subset` parameter tells `duplicated()` which columns to use when identifying duplicates.

steps.title: Detecting, dropping, and filling missing values
steps.lede: Blank cells in a DataFrame are missing values. isna detects them; dropna removes affected rows; fillna replaces them.

blocks.text: Suppose a handful of SwiftDrop orders never got a `delivery_time_minutes` recorded — those cells are just blank. Any mean or sum on that column will be wrong unless the gaps are handled first.
`isna()` (and its complement `notna()`) detects which values in a Series or DataFrame are missing: `orders["delivery_time_minutes"].isna()` returns `True` for every order missing that value.

`dropna()` removes rows that contain missing values; passing a `subset` of column labels restricts which columns are checked: `orders.dropna(subset=["delivery_time_minutes"])` removes only the orders missing that one column, ignoring gaps elsewhere.

`fillna()` replaces missing values with a specified value: `orders["delivery_time_minutes"].fillna(orders["delivery_time_minutes"].median())` replaces each missing delivery time with the column's median instead of dropping the order entirely.

before.caption: orders before handling missing values — some delivery_time_minutes are blank

after.code:
# Option A: drop rows missing delivery_time_minutes
orders_dropped = orders.dropna(subset=["delivery_time_minutes"])

# Option B: fill missing values with the column median
median_time = orders["delivery_time_minutes"].median()
orders["delivery_time_minutes"] = orders["delivery_time_minutes"].fillna(median_time)

annotations.text: dropna with subset removes only rows missing this column
fillna replaces each blank with the column's median value

blocks.change_summary: Missing delivery_time_minutes handled: either dropped with dropna(subset=...) or filled with the column median via fillna.

steps.title: Spotting and filling missing values
steps.lede: Watch isna flag blank cells and fillna replace them.

segments.label: Spotting missing values with isna() and replacing them with fillna()
segments.summary: On a small table with blank cells, isna() returns a True/False mask showing which cells pandas treats as missing, with two rows entirely missing. fillna('MISSING') replaces every missing cell with that string, while fillna(0), better suited to numeric data, replaces them with zero. The example motivation is scoring unsubmitted assignments as zeros. The inplace argument is shown as a way to make such a change permanent.

bridge.before: Watch the isna() mask and the two fillna() calls. The clip starts after its dropna steps and uses inplace=True, which Devspace's text doesn't use.
bridge.after: dropna() and its subset argument are not in this clip; Devspace's text covers them, plus filling a numeric column with its median rather than a fixed 0.

steps.title: Choosing between drop and fill
steps.lede: Test your understanding of when to use dropna versus fillna.

public.prompt: You have a DataFrame where a few rows are missing values in a numeric `delivery_time_minutes` column. You want to keep all rows but replace the missing values with a typical value. Which approach is best?

opt_a.message: Correct. `fillna()` with the median replaces missing values with a typical value from the column, preserving all rows.

opt_b.message: Not quite. `dropna()` removes rows with missing values, but the question asks to keep all rows. Use `fillna()` to replace missing values instead.

opt_c.message: Filling with 0 keeps all rows, but 0 is not a typical delivery time. Use the median to fill with a representative value: `fillna(df['delivery_time_minutes'].median())`.

opt_d.message: `isna()` detects missing values but does not replace them. Use `fillna()` to replace missing values with a typical value like the median.

correct.message: Exactly. Filling with the median preserves all rows and uses a representative value.

incorrect.message: Not quite. Review when to use `dropna()` versus `fillna()` and what value to fill with.

hints: Think about which method replaces missing values without removing rows, and what value is representative of the column.

import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv('orders_messy.csv')
required_cols = ['order_id']  # required field

# Print isna() to detect missing delivery_time_minutes
print(df['delivery_time_minutes'].isna())

# Print the column with missing value filled by its median
print(df['delivery_time_minutes'].fillna(df['delivery_time_minutes'].median()))

steps.title: Text cleaning, duplicates, and missing data — key takeaways
steps.lede: Three essential data-quality tools: .str for text, drop_duplicates for repeated rows, and isna/dropna/fillna for gaps.

blocks.text: Whatever string method you'd call on one piece of text, the `.str` accessor applies across an entire column at once. `drop_duplicates(subset=[...])` removes repeated rows by key column, keeping the first occurrence by default. Handling missing data means detecting it first with `isna()`, then deciding: drop the row if the missing field makes it unusable, or fill with a reasonable substitute such as the column's median.

blocks.title: Up next: Mapping and Applying Transformations
blocks.text: Next you'll use map substitution to replace values in a column using a lookup dict — a fast way to recode categories without writing loops.

remediation_steps.title: The .str accessor applies string methods to every row
remediation_steps.lede: Instead of looping row by row, the .str accessor vectorises any Python string method across the whole column.

blocks.text: A Series' `.str` accessor lets you call ordinary string-processing methods — matching the names of Python's built-in string methods such as `lower`, `strip`, and `replace` — on every element of the Series at once. `orders["city"].str.strip().str.lower()` removes stray whitespace and lowercases every city value in one chained call, turning `"Lagos"`, `" lagos"`, and `"LAGOS "` all into `"lagos"`.

after.code:
# With .str — one vectorised call
orders["city"] = orders["city"].str.strip().str.lower()

annotations.text: .str applies strip and lower to every element at once

blocks.change_summary: Row-by-row loop replaced by a single chained .str.strip().str.lower() call.

remediation_steps.title: Using subset to identify duplicate rows
remediation_steps.lede: drop_duplicates checks all columns by default. The subset argument limits the check to the columns that define a duplicate.

blocks.text: `duplicated()` returns a boolean vector indicating which rows are duplicates, and `drop_duplicates()` removes them; both accept a `subset` argument naming the columns used to identify a duplicated row. `orders.drop_duplicates(subset=["order_id"])` removes rows that repeat the same `order_id`, even if other columns differ slightly between the two rows.

before.code:
# Without subset — checks ALL columns; rows must be identical
orders.drop_duplicates()

annotations.text: Only removes rows where every column matches — misses partial duplicates
Removes any row whose order_id already appeared — correct for this case

blocks.change_summary: drop_duplicates called with subset=['order_id'] to catch rows with the same order ID regardless of other column differences.

remediation_steps.title: Drop or fill — choosing the right approach
remediation_steps.lede: dropna removes rows with missing values; fillna replaces them. The right choice depends on whether a reasonable substitute exists.

blocks.text: `dropna()` removes rows that contain missing values; passing a `subset` of column labels restricts which columns are checked. `fillna()` replaces missing values with a specified value. Drop the row if a missing field makes it unusable for the analysis; fill it if a reasonable substitute — such as the column's median — exists instead.

before.code:
# Missing delivery_time_minutes — two options
print(orders["delivery_time_minutes"].isna().sum())  # count of missing

annotations.text: isna().sum() counts how many values are missing

after.code:
# Drop rows where delivery_time_minutes is missing
orders_dropped = orders.dropna(subset=["delivery_time_minutes"])

# OR fill missing values with the column median
orders["delivery_time_minutes"] = orders["delivery_time_minutes"].fillna(
    orders["delivery_time_minutes"].median()
)

annotations.text: dropna removes rows missing this column
fillna replaces each blank with the median — no rows lost

blocks.change_summary: Missing delivery_time_minutes handled with either dropna (removes rows) or fillna with median (preserves rows).
